newsitem.title: FRANCE: French back euro, want Juppe sacked in 1997.
newsitem.headline: French back euro, want Juppe sacked in 1997.

text.p: French citizens start 1997 strongly in favour of a single European currency yet hoping that Prime Minister Alain Juppe, one of its main proponents in France, will lose his job, an opinion poll showed on Wednesday.
The Ifop survey, for the weekly L'Express, indicated that French people remain in a gloomy mood and doubt that record unemployment, of 12.7 percent of the workforce, will fall.
The poll showed that 79 percent thought that a European Union drive towards a single currency from 1999 would continue this year.
And 62 percent of the 803 people polled on December 27 said they hoped that progress towards the single currency would continue, against 35 percent against.
President Jacques Chirac and Juppe's centre-right government have said continued austerity is needed for France to meet the strict criteria to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU).

Fifty-five percent of those polled thought Juppe would not be in office in a year's time, against 42 percent who thought he would stay on despite record unpopularity. Juppe has said he intends to be in office for legislative elections in March 1998.
The poll showed 66 percent wanted Juppe out of office by the end of 1997, against just 30 percent who wanted him to remain.
And 55 percent said they were pessimistic about the outlook for themselves and their children, against 44 percent optimistic, identical to figures in a similar survey a year ago.
Eighty-three percent thought that unemployment would not decline in 1997.

Despite disaffection with Juppe, 53 percent believed that the opposition left would not be ready to govern after 1998 legislative elections. The Socialists were routed at the last elections in 1993, due to rising unemployment and sleaze.
